title: Section B task sheet and form conventions card
subject: English Language
source: Written for english-language/y11 lesson 43 (Section B task sheet and form conventions card (pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 43: Section B: reading a new text pair and planning the directed writing. Read the ideas from the lesson, then do the tasks.

passage.title: Text One, 'Why I Walk' (teacher-written modern column for TGA)
paras: Three years ago I sold my car. Friends assumed I had lost my job or my mind. In fact, I had simply noticed that I was spending forty minutes a day in traffic, shouting at strangers through glass.

Now I walk the two miles to work. It takes longer, of course: thirty-five minutes in good weather, forty when the rain comes sideways off the river. But those minutes are mine. I have learned the names of the streets I used to blur past. I know which bakery opens first, which tree flowers earliest in spring, which corner smells of coffee and which of wet dogs.
Walking has not made me fitter overnight; it has made me slower, and slowness turns out to be a kind of wealth. When I arrive at my desk, my head is clear.
I am not telling you to sell your car. I am asking you to try, once a week, arriving somewhere on your own two feet. You may find, as I did, that the journey was the point.

passage.title: Text Two, 'A Night Walk Through the City' (teacher-written in a nineteenth-century style for TGA)
paras: You ask how I bear the noise of London. I will confess a secret: I bear it by walking through it when it is asleep. Last night, being unable to rest, I set out at midnight and did not return until the milk-carts began their rounds.

The streets at that hour belong to a different nation. The gas-lamps burn with a sickly yellow patience; the river breathes a cold fog over the bridges; and every doorway seems to hold its breath. I passed a coffee-stall where three cab-men warmed their hands, and a watchman who wished me good night as gravely as a bishop.

I do not pretend the walk was wholly pleasant. My boots were soaked by the second mile, and twice I was startled by footsteps that proved to be my own echo. Yet I came home with a mind scrubbed clean.
Try it, dear Brother, when your country fields grow dull. A city at night will teach you more of your fellow men than a month of its daylight.

panels.title: The task
points: Your school is starting a 'Walk to Learn' week.
Write a speech for a school assembly.
Include: benefits; difficulties and how to cope; what walking teaches.

keywords.def: writing for a set task, audience and form using ideas from the texts
the type of text: speech, article, letter

questions.q: Gather six ideas (three from each text) into a grid: idea, how I will use it.
questions.a: For example: slowness as wealth; noticing streets; mind 'scrubbed clean'; discomfort (wet boots); learning about people; walking as a weekly habit.

questions.q: Decode the task: audience, form, purpose, register.
questions.a: Students; speech; persuade; semi-formal and warm.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, plan your speech (five sections) and write the opening paragraph. Starter: 'Good morning, everyone. How many of you...'
questions.a: A five-part plan covering all three bullets with ideas from both texts, and a speech opening with direct address and a hook.

questions.q: Extend: mark where each bullet point is covered in your plan.
Stretch: add one counter-argument and its answer.
questions.a: For example: 'It takes too long.' Answer: start once a week.

questions.q: Which idea from the texts is transformed best for the assembly?
options: Ten minutes on foot can clear your head before a test.
The gas-lamps burn with a sickly yellow patience.
I sold my car three years ago.
questions.a: A) Ten minutes on foot can clear your head before a test.. It turns 'my head is clear' into advice for students; the others copy details.

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: Answers vary, with an idea transformed from the texts.
